### Fig. 6: A slowdown in U.S. economic growth?

**Goal.** Look at how fast U.S. GDP per person has grown, decade by decade, since 1960.

A single year's growth jumps around with booms and recessions. To see the trend, the textbook averages
growth over the *preceding* ten years. In year $t$, with $y$ the real GDP per person,

$$\text{average growth} = 100 \times \frac{\ln y_t - \ln y_{t-10}}{10}\ \text{percent a year}.$$

We load real GDP per person for every year since 1929 and the dates of the U.S. recessions.

```{python}
gdp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "us_gdp_pc.csv")
recessions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv")
gdp.tail()
```

`gdp_pc` is real GDP per person in dollars of 2017. In `recessions`, `peak_year` and `trough_year` give the
start and end of each recession as decimal years (1960.25 is April 1960).

> **Python note.** `gdp.copy()` makes a copy of the table, so that adding a column inside the function
> leaves `gdp` itself unchanged. `.shift(window)` moves a column down by `window` rows, so in each row it gives the value
> from `window` years earlier. `np.log` is the natural logarithm. The `for` loop with `zip` hands over one
> (start, end) pair of each recession at a time, and `fig.add_vrect` shades the band between them.

```{python}
def slowdown_chart(window=10):
    """Fig. 6.6: average annual growth of U.S. GDP per person over the preceding `window` years."""
    table = gdp.copy()
    table["growth"] = 100 * (np.log(table.gdp_pc) - np.log(table.gdp_pc.shift(window))) / window
    table = table[table.year >= 1960]
    before = table[table.year <= 2006].growth.mean()
    since = table[table.year >= 2009].growth.mean()
    fig = px.line(table, x="year", y="growth",
                  labels={"year": "Year", "growth": f"{window}-year average growth (%)"},
                  title=f"{window}-year average growth of GDP per person: {before:.1f}% in 1960–2006, "
                        f"{since:.1f}% since 2009")
    fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3))
    for start, end in zip(recessions.peak_year, recessions.trough_year):
        fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=BLUE, opacity=0.12, line_width=0)
    fig.update_layout(yaxis_range=[-0.5, 4.5], xaxis_range=[1959, 2026])
    return fig
```

> **Python note.** A `Dropdown` is a menu of choices. Here it sets the number of years in the average.

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(slowdown_chart,
         window=Dropdown(options=[5, 10, 15, 20], value=10, description="years in the average", style=WIDE));
```

```{python}
slider_figure(slowdown_chart, "window", [5, 10, 15, 20], start=10, label="years in the average")
```

**Sources.** Data: [U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Real Gross Domestic Product (`GDPCA`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPCA) and [U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Population (`B230RC0A052NBEA`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/B230RC0A052NBEA); recessions from the [NBER based Recession Indicators (`USREC`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/USREC), which follow the [NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee](https://www.nber.org/research/business-cycle-dating).
Prepared files: [`data/ch06/us_gdp_pc.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch06/us_gdp_pc.csv), [`data/ch06/recessions.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch06/recessions.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch06/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 6.6 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- From 1960 to 2006 the 10-year average moved between about 1.2 and 3.4 percent, around a fairly
  stable mean of 2.2 percent. After the Great Recession of 2007–2009 it fell below 1 percent.
- The textbook's data end in 2018. With seven more years, the 10-year average has recovered to about
  1.8 percent, still below the pre-2007 mean.
- Shorter windows (5 years) show more ups and downs; longer windows (20 years) smooth them away.

<!-- cell -->

#### Key numbers: the slowdown and growth accounting (Table 6.2)

```{python}
ten = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig6-6.csv").set_index("year").gdp_pc_growth_10yr
print(f"Mean 1960-2006: {ten.loc[1960:2006].mean():.2f}%   (range {ten.loc[1960:2006].min():.2f} to {ten.loc[1960:2006].max():.2f})")
print(f"Mean 2009-2018: {ten.loc[2009:2018].mean():.2f}%   (lowest: {ten.min():.2f} in {ten.idxmin()})")
print(f"1983: {ten[1983]:.2f}%   1985: {ten[1985]:.2f}%   (the quick rebound after 1982)")
print(f"2019-2025:", ten.loc[2019:2025].round(2).tolist())
```

What is behind the slowdown? **Growth accounting** splits the growth of output per hour into three parts,
using the production function $Y_t = A_tK_t^{1/3}L_{yt}^{2/3}$ (equation 10, derived in "Model overview"):

$$\underbrace{g_{Y}-g_{L}}_{\text{output per hour}} = \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{3}(g_{K}-g_{L})}_{\text{capital per hour}} + \underbrace{\tfrac{2}{3}(g_{L_y}-g_{L})}_{\text{labor composition}} + \underbrace{g_{A}}_{\text{TFP}}$$

The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes an index for each of the four terms. The average growth of an
index between years $a$ and $b$ is $100 \times \ln(X_b/X_a)/(b-a)$.

> **Python note.** `.loc[end]` picks the row of one year. Dividing two rows divides them column by column,
> so one line computes the growth of all four indexes. A dictionary of columns then becomes a table.

```{python}
accounts = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "growth_accounting.csv").set_index("year")


def period_growth(start, end):
    """Average annual growth (percent, log points) of every index from start to end (Table 6.2)."""
    return 100 * np.log(accounts.loc[end] / accounts.loc[start]) / (end - start)


columns = {}
for start, end in [(1948, 2021), (1948, 1973), (1973, 1995), (1995, 2003), (2003, 2021), (2003, 2025)]:
    columns[f"{start}–{end}"] = period_growth(start, end)
table62 = pd.DataFrame(columns)
table62.index = ["Output per hour, Y/L", "Contribution of K/L", "Labor composition", "Contribution of TFP, A"]
table62.round(1)
```

The textbook's Table 6.2 for comparison (the last column is new):

```{python}
book = pd.DataFrame({"1948–2021": [2.4, 0.9, 0.2, 1.2], "1948–1973": [3.3, 1.0, 0.2, 2.1],
                     "1973–1995": [1.5, 0.8, 0.2, 0.5], "1995–2003": [3.2, 1.4, 0.3, 1.5],
                     "2003–2021": [1.8, 0.8, 0.3, 0.7]}, index=table62.index)
book
```

Where do our numbers differ from the book's? We subtract the two tables (rounded to one decimal) and
check that the three contributions add up to the growth of output per hour, as equation (10) says.

```{python}
print("Our table minus the book's table:")
print(table62[book.columns].round(1) - book)
gap = table62.iloc[1:].sum() - table62.iloc[0]      # contributions minus output per hour, every period
print(f"\nLargest gap between the sum of contributions and output per hour: {gap.abs().max():.3f}")
```

Only three cells differ, by 0.1 point each, because the BLS has revised its data since the book was
written: TFP growth over 1948–2021, and output per hour and TFP over 2003–2021. The productivity slowdown after 1973 and the new slowdown after 2003 are both
mostly slowdowns in **TFP growth**, the part that the Romer model attributes to new ideas.

<!-- cell -->

#### Beyond the United States

Was the slowdown an American story? The Penn World Table (PWT) measures real GDP per person for 185
countries since 1950, in 2021 U.S. dollars. A wider file holds it, one row per country and year, with the
country's World Bank region.

```{python}
world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gdp_pc_countries.csv")
world.head()
```

Many series start later than 1950: in 1960, 1970, or 1990 for the former Soviet and Yugoslav republics. So
a country's 10-year average appears only ten years after its data start. For the United States, the PWT
growth rates differ from the BEA numbers above by at most 0.2 points.

> **Python note.** `growth_table` loops over the chosen countries, computes each one's growth with
> `.shift(window)` as before, and joins the pieces with `pd.concat`. `.groupby("country").last()` keeps
> each country's latest row, and `.idxmax()` gives the country with the highest growth. `set(a) - set(b)`
> lists the names in `a` that are not in `b`: here, the countries with no data. `round(x, 1) + 0.0` turns a
> rounded −0.0 into 0.0.

```{python}
ALL_COUNTRIES = sorted(world.country.unique())
GROWTH_REGIONS = dict(zip(world.country, world.region))
GROWTH_SHOWN = ["United States", "China", "India"]          # the website's default view, colored first
COUNTRY_COLORS = group_colors(GROWTH_SHOWN + ALL_COUNTRIES, region_groups(GROWTH_REGIONS, GROWTH_SHOWN),
                              {"United States": BLUE})


def growth_table(names, window):
    """Average growth of GDP per person over the preceding `window` years, chosen countries, 1960 on."""
    pieces = [world.head(0)]                    # an empty table to start with, so concat always works
    for name in names:
        one = world[world.country == name].copy()
        one["growth"] = 100 * (np.log(one.gdp_pc) - np.log(one.gdp_pc.shift(window))) / window
        pieces.append(one[one.year >= 1960].dropna(subset=["growth"]))
    return pd.concat(pieces)
```

```{python}
def growth_by_country(names=("United States",), window=10):
    """Fig. 6.6 for any countries: the latest highest and lowest growth in the title."""
    table = growth_table(names, window)
    if len(table) == 0:
        return go.Figure(layout=dict(title=f"No {window}-year growth rates for: " + (", ".join(names) or "pick a country")))
    latest = table.groupby("country").last()
    fast, slow = latest.growth.idxmax(), latest.growth.idxmin()
    title = f"{window}-year growth in {latest.year.max()}: {fast} {round(latest.growth[fast], 1) + 0.0:.1f}%"
    if slow != fast:
        title = title + f", {slow} {round(latest.growth[slow], 1) + 0.0:.1f}%"
    missing = sorted(set(names) - set(table.country))
    if missing:
        title = title + " (no data: " + ", ".join(missing) + ")"
    fig = px.line(table, x="year", y="growth", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=COUNTRY_COLORS, title=title,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "growth": f"{window}-year average growth (%)", "country": "Country"})
    for low, high in [(-0.5, 4.5), (-2.5, 10.5), (-10.5, 20.5), (-40.5, 40.5)]:   # widen only when needed
        if table.growth.min() >= low and table.growth.max() <= high:
            break
    fig.update_layout(yaxis_range=[low, high], xaxis_range=[1959, 2024])
    fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=[1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020])      # no label at the bottom-left corner
    return fig
```

## Fixed costs in practice: software

A worked exercise applies the economics of ideas to a product with a huge development cost and almost no cost per copy.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 7: The word processor production function

**Goal.** Apply the economics of ideas to software: a large fixed cost and a tiny marginal cost.

This figure comes from a worked exercise in the textbook. A word processor with perfect speech
recognition costs \$100 million to create, and each copy then costs \$1 to distribute. With $X$
million dollars spent, the number of copies (in millions) is

$$Y = X - 100 \quad \text{for } X > 100, \qquad Y = 0 \text{ otherwise.}$$

If the firm sells copies at a price $p$ above the marginal cost of \$1, it **breaks even** when revenue
covers the total cost: $pY = 100 + Y$, so $Y = 100/(p-1)$ million copies.

```{python}
def word_processor(F=100.0, p=20.0):
    """Fig. 6.7: copies (millions) against spending X (millions of $), fixed cost F, $1 per copy."""
    X = np.linspace(0, 320, 321)
    copies = np.maximum(X - F, 0)                    # nothing until the program exists
    breakeven = F / (p - 1)                          # copies needed to cover all costs at price p
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=X, y=copies, name="Production function", line=dict(color=TEAL, width=4)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[F + breakeven], y=[breakeven], name=f"Break-even point at a price of {p:.0f} dollars",
                             mode="markers", marker=dict(color="black", size=12)))
    x_max, y_max = 210, 105
    if F + breakeven > 200:                          # widen the axes only when the break-even point is far out
        x_max, y_max = 320, 160
    fig.update_layout(title=f"At a price of {p:.0f} dollars a copy, the firm breaks even at {breakeven:.2f} million copies",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Input, X (millions of dollars)", range=[0, x_max],
                                 tickvals=list(range(50, x_max, 50))),  # no corner label
                      yaxis=dict(title="Output, Y (millions of copies)", range=[0, y_max]))
    return fig
```

**Source.** Adapted from Fig. 6.7 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612), which illustrates a worked exercise.

**What to notice.**

- The production function is flat at zero up to \$100 million and then rises one for one. It "curves
  up" from the origin: spending \$200 million gives 100 million copies, but spending half as much gives
  none at all. That is increasing returns.
- At a price of \$20 the firm needs 5.26 million copies to break even; at \$100 it needs only 1.01 million.
- At a price of \$2 the break-even point is at 100 million copies: the firm can survive at a low price
  only if the market is huge. **Scale matters.**

## Combining Solow and Romer

Finally, we put capital back into the model. Ideas still drive long-run growth, while the investment rate moves the level of the growth path.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 8: Output after a rise in the investment rate

**Goal.** Combine the two models: a Solow economy with capital that sits on top of the Romer
growth in ideas. Then raise the investment rate.

The combined model (the textbook's appendix to this chapter) adds capital to the Romer model. Output is
$Y_t = A_t^{\gamma}K_t^{1/3}L_{yt}^{2/3}$, capital accumulates as in Chapter 5,
$\Delta K_{t+1} = \bar{s}Y_t - \bar{d}K_t$, and ideas, workers and population follow the Romer
equations. On the balanced growth path (equations 7 and 9),

$$g_y^* = \tfrac{3}{2}\gamma\bar{n} \qquad\qquad y_t^* = \left(\frac{\bar{s}}{g_Y^* + \bar{d}}\right)^{1/2} \left(A_t^*\right)^{3\gamma/2}(1-\bar{\ell})$$

where $g_Y^* = g_y^* + \bar{n}$ is the growth of total output. (The textbook prints the level for the case
$\gamma = 1$, where the exponent on $A_t^*$ is $3/2$.) Growth is *faster* than in the Romer
model: ideas raise output, the extra output is partly invested, and the extra capital raises
output again. A higher investment rate $\bar{s}$ raises the **level** of the BGP, not its growth rate.

The function below is the combined model's version of `simulate_romer`. In yearly steps, output per
person on the BGP grows by the factor $(1+\bar{n})^{3\gamma/2}$, which is close to $1 + \tfrac{3}{2}\gamma\bar{n}$.

```{python}
def simulate_combined(s_old=0.05, s_new=0.05, gamma=2 / 3, n=0.03, d=0.02, z=1.0, l=0.1,
                      change_year=2050, first_year=2025, last_year=2100):
    """Combined Solow-Romer model year by year (equations 7 to 9 on its BGP); s changes to s_new in change_year."""
    years = np.arange(first_year, last_year + 1)
    g_y = (1 + n) ** (1.5 * gamma) - 1              # BGP growth of output per person, yearly steps
    g_Y = (1 + g_y) * (1 + n) - 1                   # BGP growth of total output
    N = 1.0
    A = z * l * N / n                               # BGP stock of ideas, as in the Romer model
    K = (s_old / (g_Y + d)) ** 1.5 * A ** (1.5 * gamma) * (1 - l) * N   # BGP capital, from equation (8)
    y_path, bgp_path = [], []
    for year in years:
        if year < change_year:
            s = s_old
        else:
            s = s_new
        Y = A ** gamma * K ** (1 / 3) * ((1 - l) * N) ** (2 / 3)        # output: the production function
        y_path.append(Y / N)
        bgp_path.append((s / (g_Y + d)) ** 0.5 * A ** (1.5 * gamma) * (1 - l))   # BGP level, equation (9)
        K = K + s * Y - d * K                       # capital accumulation
        A = A + z * l * N                           # new ideas
        N = N * (1 + n)                             # population growth
    scale = 1 / y_path[0]                           # normalization: y = 1 in the first year
    return years, scale * np.array(y_path), scale * np.array(bgp_path)
```

```{python}
def rise_in_s(s_old=0.05, s_new=0.6, scale="ratio"):
    """Fig. 6.8: output per person when the investment rate rises from s_old to s_new in 2050."""
    years, y, y_bgp = simulate_combined(s_old=s_old, s_new=s_new)
    years, y_old, y_old_bgp = simulate_combined(s_old=s_old, s_new=s_old)   # the old balanced growth path
    level = y_bgp[-1] / y_old[-1]
    fig = experiment_chart(years, y, y_old, y_bgp, scale)
    # y[25] is 2050, y[26] is 2051 and y[-1] is the last year, 2100
    fig.update_layout(title=f"New BGP ×{level:.2f} the old | growth {100 * (y[26] / y[25] - 1):.1f}% in 2051, "
                            f"{100 * (y[-1] / y[-2] - 1):.1f}% in 2100 (BGP: {100 * (y[1] / y[0] - 1):.1f}%)")
    return fig
```

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- Before 2050 output per person grows at 3 percent a year, which is $\tfrac{3}{2}\gamma\bar{n}$ with
  $\gamma = 2/3$ and $\bar{n} = 0.03$. In the Romer model with the same parameters it would be only 2 percent.
- In 2050 the investment rate jumps from 0.05 to 0.6. Output does not jump, because the capital stock
  needs time to grow, but growth rises at once to about 26 percent, then slows back toward 3 percent.
- In the long run, output per person is $\sqrt{0.6/0.05} \approx 3.46$ times higher: a level effect,
  just like in the Solow model. The long-run growth rate is still set by ideas.

## Concluding remarks

- Romer divides goods into **objects** and **ideas**. Ideas are **nonrival**: they can be used by any
  number of people at once, so there are constant returns to objects and **increasing returns** to objects
  and ideas together, equation (1).
- Increasing returns come with fixed research costs. If prices equaled marginal cost, nobody could pay
  for research, so innovation needs patents, secrecy, public funding or prizes.
- In the **Romer model**, income per person depends on the total stock of ideas, equation (2), and the stock
  of ideas is proportional to the number of researchers, equation (3). On the balanced growth path the level is
  equation (4) and long-run growth is $g_y^* = \gamma\bar{n}$, equation (5). Changes in research productivity
  or the research share have **level effects** and transition dynamics (equation 6), but leave long-run growth unchanged.
- The **combined Solow–Romer model** grows at $\tfrac{3}{2}\gamma\bar{n}$, equation (7): capital amplifies the growth of ideas.
  Investment rates and other Solow parameters set the capital-output ratio and the level of the BGP, equations (8)
  and (9), and the principle of transition dynamics explains why countries grow at different rates for decades.
- **Growth accounting**, equation (10), splits the growth of output per hour into capital, labor composition
  and TFP; in the U.S. data, the productivity slowdowns are mostly TFP slowdowns.
- The next chapter turns from long-run growth to the **labor market**: wages and unemployment.

Each problem is marked Basic, Intermediate or Challenge; try it on your own first, then open the Hint, and open the Solution last. <!-- cell -->

### Conceptual problems

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 1 (Basic): Paying for an antibiotic that doctors keep in reserve.** Doctors are asked to save new antibiotics for the infections that older drugs no longer cure, so that bacteria do not become resistant to them as well. That is good for patients, but it keeps sales small. In a pilot, England's National Health Service started in July 2022 to pay companies a fixed yearly fee for two new antibiotics, based on their value to the health service rather than on the number of doses used, and it has since opened the scheme to more drugs ([NHS England](https://www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/antimicrobial-products-subscription-model-guidance-on-commercial-arrangements/)). Use the numbers of Fig. 1: a research cost $\bar{F}$ of 2.5 billion dollars and a marginal cost $c$ of 10 dollars a dose.

(a) A hypothetical reserve antibiotic sells 50 million doses over its patent life, and a hypothetical common antibiotic sells 1 billion doses. At what price per dose does each firm just break even?

(b) Under a subscription, the health service buys the doses at their marginal cost and adds a fixed fee every year for 10 years. How large must the yearly fee be for the maker of the reserve antibiotic to break even? (Ignore interest.)

(c) Why does a fixed fee suit a drug that should be used sparingly better than a high price per dose? In England, the highest fee band is £20 million a year per drug ([The Pharmaceutical Journal](https://pharmaceutical-journal.com/article/feature/everything-you-need-to-know-about-the-nhs-antimicrobial-resistance-subscription-model)). Compare it with your answer to (b): what does nonrivalry suggest about who should pay for the research?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Use the break-even price of the Model overview, $p = c + \bar{F}/Y$. With $\bar{F}$ in millions of dollars and $Y$ in millions of doses, the units match. In (b), doses sold at marginal cost just pay for their own production, so the fees must cover something else.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The break-even price is marginal cost plus the research cost per dose sold:

$$p_{\text{reserve}} = 10 + \frac{2{,}500}{50} = 10 + 50 = 60 \text{ dollars}, \qquad p_{\text{common}} = 10 + \frac{2{,}500}{1{,}000} = 10 + 2.5 = 12.50 \text{ dollars}.$$

Both drugs cost the same to invent, but the reserve drug spreads that cost over 20 times fewer doses, so each dose must carry 50 dollars of research cost instead of 2.50. Scale matters: a small market makes a nonrival idea expensive per unit.

**(b)** At $p = c$ the revenue from doses equals their production cost, so profit is the fees minus the research cost. Breaking even over 10 years needs $10 \times \text{fee} = 2{,}500$ million dollars, a fee of **250 million dollars a year**.

**(c)**

- With a fixed fee, the firm's income no longer rises with the number of doses, so it gains nothing from pushing sales. That is exactly what doctors who keep the drug in reserve want.
- The doses are sold at marginal cost, so no hospital is priced out when a patient really needs the drug: the wedge between price and marginal cost, and its cost (see "What the model predicts" in the economics of ideas), disappears. The research is paid for by taxpayers instead of by sick patients.
- The formula of an antibiotic is nonrival: once it is discovered, it can cure patients in every country at once. A fee of £20 million a year is a small fraction of the 250 million dollars a year in (b), because England is only a small part of the world market. If each country pays only for its own patients and waits for others to pay for the research, too little research gets done. A nonrival idea is best paid for jointly, for example through similar fees in many countries.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 2 (Intermediate): Why did U.S. productivity growth slow down after 1973?** The BLS growth-accounting data of Fig. 6 give these averages, in percent a year (the table `table62` above, rounded):

| Period | Output per hour | Capital per hour | Labor composition | TFP |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1948–1973 | 3.3 | 1.0 | 0.2 | 2.1 |
| 1973–1995 | 1.5 | 0.8 | 0.2 | 0.5 |

(a) By how many points did the growth of output per hour fall from the first period to the second? How much of that fall does growth accounting, equation (10), assign to TFP, and how much to capital per hour?

(b) Now use the combined Solow–Romer model with $\gamma = 1$, so that $A_t$ is TFP, and leave labor composition aside. On a balanced growth path, how fast does output per hour grow when TFP grows by 2.1 percent a year, and when it grows by 0.5 percent? How much of each would growth accounting credit to capital per hour? Compare your first answer with the 1948–1973 row.

(c) In the model, how much of the long-run slowdown is caused by slower TFP growth? Why is this more than the share you found in (a)?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

In (b), equation (7) with $\gamma = 1$ links the growth of output per hour to TFP growth. On a balanced growth path, capital per hour grows as fast as output per hour, and it enters equation (10) with the weight 1/3.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Output per hour slowed by $3.3 - 1.5 = 1.8$ points. TFP growth fell by $2.1 - 0.5 = 1.6$ points and the contribution of capital per hour by $1.0 - 0.8 = 0.2$ points; labor composition did not change. Growth accounting therefore assigns $1.6/1.8 \approx 89$ percent of the slowdown to TFP.

**(b)** With $\gamma = 1$, equation (7) says $g_y^* = \tfrac{3}{2}g_A$, and on the balanced growth path capital per hour grows at the same rate as output per hour.

- TFP growth of 2.1 percent: $g_y^* = 1.5 \times 2.1 = 3.15$ percent a year. Growth accounting credits capital per hour with $\tfrac{1}{3}\times 3.15 = 1.05$ points and TFP with 2.1 points.
- TFP growth of 0.5 percent: $g_y^* = 1.5 \times 0.5 = 0.75$ percent a year, of which $\tfrac{1}{3}\times 0.75 = 0.25$ points are credited to capital.

In 1948–1973, output per hour grew by $3.3 - 0.2 = 3.1$ percent a year once labor composition is left aside, and capital contributed 1.0 point. Both are very close to the model's 3.15 and 1.05: the postwar U.S. economy looks like a balanced growth path driven by TFP.

**(c)** In the model, the long-run slowdown is $3.15 - 0.75 = 2.4$ points, and **all of it** is caused by slower TFP growth: 1.6 points directly, and $1.05 - 0.25 = 0.8$ points because capital per hour grows more slowly once TFP does. Growth accounting books those 0.8 points under capital. But in the model capital per hour keeps growing only because TFP growth keeps raising output and so the amount worth investing. This is the sense in which accounting is not causation. In the data for 1973–1995, capital per hour still contributed 0.8 points, far more than the 0.25 of the new balanced growth path: the capital stock adjusts slowly (transition dynamics), so output per hour fell by 1.8 points in that period rather than by the full 2.4.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 3 (Challenge): Are ideas getting harder to find?** Moore's law says that the number of transistors on a computer chip doubles about every two years, a steady growth rate of about 35 percent a year. Bloom, Jones, Van Reenen and Webb (2020), ["Are Ideas Getting Harder to Find?"](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20180338), *American Economic Review* 110(4), find that the research effort behind it rose by a factor of 18 from 1971 to 2014, while that growth rate stayed about the same. Call the growth rate of ideas per researcher, $g_{At}/L_{at}$, **research productivity**.

(a) In the Romer model, use the production of ideas to show that research productivity equals $\bar{z}/A_t$. How fast does it change on the balanced growth path?

(b) Chip density kept growing at a constant rate while research effort rose 18-fold over the 43 years from 1971 to 2014. By what factor did research productivity fall, and at what average rate per year? Use $100\times\ln(\text{factor})/43$.

(c) In Romer's original version, $\Delta A_{t+1}/A_t = \bar{z}L_{at}$ (see the Model overview). What growth rate of chip density would that version predict after an 18-fold rise in research effort? Which version fits the facts?

(d) Is the finding that ideas get harder to find bad news for the model of this chapter? What change in the world would make it bad news for long-run growth?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

(a) Divide both sides of $\Delta A_{t+1} = \bar{z}L_{at}$ by $A_t$, and then by $L_{at}$. (b) Write research productivity in 1971 and in 2014 as the growth rate of chip density divided by research effort, and divide one by the other. (d) Look at $g_{At} = \bar{z}\bar{\ell}N_t/A_t$ from step 3 of the Romer model when $N_t$ stops growing.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Divide the production of ideas by $A_t$, and then by $L_{at}$:

$$g_{At} = \frac{\Delta A_{t+1}}{A_t} = \frac{\bar{z}L_{at}}{A_t} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{g_{At}}{L_{at}} = \frac{\bar{z}}{A_t}.$$

$\bar{z}$ is constant and the stock of ideas only grows, so research productivity falls every year: from one year to the next it is multiplied by $A_t/A_{t+1} = 1/(1+g_{At})$. On the balanced growth path $g_A^* = \bar{n}$, so research productivity falls at about the rate $\bar{n}$, exactly as fast as the number of researchers grows. Each researcher still adds $\bar{z}$ ideas a year, but each new idea is a smaller percentage of an ever larger stock.

**(b)** The growth rate stayed the same while the number of researchers rose 18-fold, so the growth rate per researcher fell by a **factor of 18**. Per year, that is $100\times\ln 18/43 = 100 \times 2.890/43 \approx 6.7$ log points. (The authors report about 6.8 percent a year; their factor is a little more than 18.)

**(c)** In the original version, the growth rate of ideas is proportional to the number of researchers. With 18 times as many researchers, chip density would grow $18 \times 35 = 630$ percent a year instead of 35 percent. Instead, the growth rate stayed at about 35 percent. The chapter's version fits: $g_{At} = \bar{z}L_{at}/A_t$ stays constant when researchers and ideas grow at the same rate.

**(d)** It is not bad news for the model: it is what the model predicts. On the balanced growth path, research productivity $\bar{z}/A_t$ falls at the rate $\bar{n}$, and steady growth needs a research workforce that keeps growing. The same paper finds the pattern for the U.S. economy as a whole: since the 1930s, research effort has grown by 4.3 percent a year, while research productivity has fallen by 5.1 percent a year. It would be bad news if the number of researchers stopped growing. With $N_t$ constant, $g_{At} = \bar{z}\bar{\ell}N_t/A_t$ falls toward zero as $A_t$ keeps rising, and so does the growth of income per person, $g_{yt} = \gamma g_{At}$. In this model, slower growth of the world's population, and so of its researchers, is a threat to long-run growth.

</details>

**Problem 4 (Basic): Growth miracles and growth disasters.** The file `gdp_pc_countries.csv` holds real GDP per person for 185 countries from the [Penn World Table 11.0](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/) (Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer 2015).

(a) Keep the countries with data in both 1960 and 2023, and compute each one's average growth rate of GDP per person, $100\times\ln(y_{2023}/y_{1960})/63$ percent a year. Which five countries grew fastest, and which five grew slowest?

(b) How many of these countries were poorer in 2023 than in 1960?

(c) Before you trust a ranking, look at the levels. Sort the countries by GDP per person in 2023: which number is not plausible?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

If you load the file as `pwt`, then `pwt.pivot(index="country", columns="year", values="gdp_pc")` gives a table with one row per country and one column per year. Keep the columns 1960 and 2023 with `[[1960, 2023]]`, and drop the countries with a missing value with `.dropna()`. A negative growth rate means that the country became poorer.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

Load the file, turn it into one row per country, keep the two years, compute the growth rates and sort them.

```python
pwt = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gdp_pc_countries.csv")
wide = pwt.pivot(index="country", columns="year", values="gdp_pc")
both = wide[[1960, 2023]].dropna()                    # countries with data in both years
growth = 100 * np.log(both[2023] / both[1960]) / 63   # percent a year
print(len(growth), "countries")
print(growth.sort_values(ascending=False).head(5).round(2))
print(growth.sort_values().head(5).round(2))
print("Poorer in 2023 than in 1960:", (growth < 0).sum())
print(both.sort_values(2023).head(3).round(1))
```

- **(a)** Of the 111 countries, the fastest growers are China (6.12 percent a year), Taiwan (5.44 percent), South Korea (5.38 percent), Singapore (4.61 percent) and Malta (4.53 percent). The slowest are DR Congo (−1.47), Venezuela (−1.19), the Central African Republic (−0.92), Madagascar (−0.78) and Niger (−0.42).
- **(b)** Six countries were poorer in 2023 than in 1960: those five and Guinea-Bissau.
- **(c)** Venezuela's GDP per person in 2023 is 187.4 dollars, less than a fifth of the next lowest value among the countries of (a) (Burundi, 976.8 dollars). As in [Chapter 5](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/ch05-the-solow-growth-model.html), the price data behind this level broke down during Venezuela's hyperinflation, so it should be dropped. Without it, the slowest five are DR Congo, the Central African Republic, Madagascar, Niger and Guinea-Bissau.

Growing at 6.1 percent a year for 63 years multiplied China's GDP per person by about 47 (from 463 to 21,825 dollars), while DR Congo's fell by about 60 percent. In the combined model, decades of growth this fast or this slow are transition dynamics: the fastest growers raised their balanced growth paths (for example by investing more, as Problem 7 shows for South Korea) and grew fast while they caught up, while the paths of the slowest economies fell.

</details>

**Problem 5 (Intermediate): Which raw materials became cheaper?** The file `commodity_prices.csv` holds the real prices of 40 commodities, with 1900 = 100, from Jacks (2019), ["From Boom to Bust"](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11698-018-0173-5), extended with the [World Bank's Pink Sheet](https://www.worldbank.org/en/research/commodity-markets). Ten of the series stop in 2020, so compare 1900 with 2020.

(a) For each commodity, compute the average yearly change in its real price, $100\times\ln(p_{2020}/p_{1900})/120$ percent a year. How many of the 40 became cheaper?

(b) Average these rates within each group (column `group`). Which groups became cheaper fastest, and which became more expensive?

(c) 2020 was the first year of the pandemic, an unusual year for prices. Redo the count with the average prices of 1900–1904 and of 2016–2020, which are 116 years apart. Does the main finding survive?

(d) The world economy grew many times over during these 120 years. What does the Romer model suggest about why most of these prices fell anyway?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Make a table with one column per commodity with `pivot`, as in the cell that checked the Simon–Ehrlich bet. Then `table.loc[2020] / table.loc[1900]` divides two rows, one commodity at a time. For (b), put the rates and the groups side by side in a DataFrame and use `.groupby("group")`.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

Build the table, compute one rate per commodity, then average the rates by group.

```python
jacks = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "commodity_prices.csv")
table = jacks.pivot(index="year", columns="commodity", values="real_price_1900_100")
groups = jacks.drop_duplicates("commodity").set_index("commodity").group
rate = 100 * np.log(table.loc[2020] / table.loc[1900]) / 120
print("Cheaper in 2020 than in 1900:", (rate < 0).sum(), "of", len(rate))
summary = pd.DataFrame({"rate": rate, "group": groups})
print(summary.groupby("group").rate.mean().sort_values().round(2))
print(rate[rate > 0].sort_values().round(2))
first5 = table.loc[1900:1904].mean()                  # average price in 1900-1904
last5 = table.loc[2016:2020].mean()                   # average price in 2016-2020
rate5 = 100 * np.log(last5 / first5) / 116
print("Cheaper with five-year averages:", (rate5 < 0).sum(), "of", len(rate5))
summary5 = pd.DataFrame({"rate": rate5, "group": groups})
print(summary5.groupby("group").rate.mean().sort_values().round(2))
```

- **(a)** 32 of the 40 commodities were cheaper in real terms in 2020 than in 1900. Rubber (−2.57 percent a year) and aluminum (−2.29) fell fastest. Wheat fell by 1.11 percent a year, so after 120 years it cost about a quarter of its 1900 price.
- **(b)** By group, softs (−1.16 percent a year), minerals (−1.06) and grains (−1.02) became cheaper fastest, followed by animal products (−0.61) and metals (−0.44). Energy (+0.30) and precious metals (+0.41) became more expensive. The eight commodities that rose are manganese, chromium, coal, platinum, lamb, beef, petroleum and gold (+0.83 percent a year); silver and iron ore barely changed.
- **(c)** With five-year averages, 30 of the 40 became cheaper, and the groups keep their signs: grains (−1.13), softs (−1.11), minerals (−0.93), animal products (−0.53) and metals (−0.36) fell, while precious metals (+0.33) and energy (+0.57) rose. The main finding does not depend on the pandemic year.
- **(d)** Demand for raw materials rose enormously, so with fixed technology their prices should have risen. In the Romer model, new ideas keep arriving: better ways to find, mine, grow and use resources, and substitutes for them. Each of these ideas is nonrival, so it raises the output of every mine and every farm at once, and supply grew faster than demand. Energy and precious metals are the exceptions in our data.

</details>

**Problem 6 (Challenge): Do poor countries catch up?** In the combined Solow–Romer model, every country grows at the rate of world ideas in the long run, but a country far below its own balanced growth path grows faster for a while. If poor countries were simply further below similar paths, they would grow faster than rich ones and catch up: **convergence**. Test this with the Penn World Table file of Problem 4, leaving out Venezuela.

(a) For the countries with data in 1960, compute the correlation between the log of GDP per person in 1960 and the average growth rate from 1960 to 1990.

(b) For the same countries, compute the correlation between the log of GDP per person in 2000 and the average growth rate from 2000 to 2023.

(c) Repeat (a) for the countries in the region Europe & Central Asia.

(d) What do the signs tell you? Use the principle of transition dynamics to explain the difference between (a) and (c), and suggest what may have changed after 2000.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

A negative correlation means that the countries that started poorer grew faster. `np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]` gives the correlation of two columns, and `.isin(names)` keeps the rows of the listed countries. In the model, each country converges to its *own* balanced growth path, which depends on its investment rate and its access to ideas.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

Keep the countries that have all four years, compute the two growth rates, and correlate each one with the log of the starting level.

```python
pwt = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "gdp_pc_countries.csv")
pwt = pwt[pwt.country != "Venezuela"]                 # implausible levels (Problem 4)
wide = pwt.pivot(index="country", columns="year", values="gdp_pc")
sample = wide[[1960, 1990, 2000, 2023]].dropna()      # the countries with data in 1960
early = 100 * np.log(sample[1990] / sample[1960]) / 30
late = 100 * np.log(sample[2023] / sample[2000]) / 23
print(len(sample), "countries")
print(f"1960-1990: correlation {np.corrcoef(np.log(sample[1960]), early)[0, 1]:.2f}")
print(f"2000-2023: correlation {np.corrcoef(np.log(sample[2000]), late)[0, 1]:.2f}")
names = pwt[pwt.region == "Europe & Central Asia"].country.unique()
europe = sample[sample.index.isin(names)]
europe_growth = 100 * np.log(europe[1990] / europe[1960]) / 30
print(len(europe), "countries in Europe & Central Asia")
print(f"1960-1990: correlation {np.corrcoef(np.log(europe[1960]), europe_growth)[0, 1]:.2f}")
```

- **(a)** For the 110 countries, the correlation is **+0.12**. The poorer countries of 1960 did not grow faster on average; if anything, they grew a little more slowly.
- **(b)** For the same 110 countries, the correlation from 2000 to 2023 is **−0.33**: this time, poorer countries grew faster.
- **(c)** For the 21 countries of Europe & Central Asia with data in 1960, the correlation is **−0.82**. Portugal, Greece and Spain, for example, grew much faster than Switzerland.
- **(d)** The principle of transition dynamics says that a country grows faster the further it is below **its own** balanced growth path. In 1960–1990, those paths differed a lot across the world, because investment rates, education, institutions and access to world ideas differed. Many poor countries were poor because their paths were low, so they had no reason to grow fast. The European countries had similar parameters, so the poorer ones were further below similar paths and caught up. After 2000, the negative correlation suggests that the parameters of many poorer countries improved, which raised their paths and opened gaps that brought fast growth (China and India are examples), while growth at the frontier slowed (Fig. 6). Kremer, Willis and You (2021), ["Converging to Convergence"](https://www.nber.org/papers/w29484), document the same trend toward convergence since 2000, and find that human capital, policies and institutions converged across countries over the same period, toward the levels found in richer countries.

</details>

Take a stylized version in the combined model of Fig. 8: an economy on its balanced growth path raises its investment rate from 0.10 to 0.40 in 2050. A minister claims that the new rate will keep growth high for ever.

(a) Set the new investment rate to 0.40. How fast does output per person grow in 2051 and in 2100? How much higher is the new BGP than the old one?

(b) Is the minister right? Explain with equations (7) and (9) and the principle of transition dynamics.

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** With $\bar{s}' = 0.40$ the title reads "New BGP ×2.00 the old | growth 10.3% in 2051, 3.2% in 2100 (BGP: 3.0%)". Output per person grows by 10.3 percent in 2051 and by 3.2 percent in 2100, and the new BGP is twice the old one. Equation (9) gives the same factor: $y_t^*$ is proportional to $\bar{s}^{1/2}$, and $(0.40/0.10)^{1/2} = \sqrt{4} = 2$. The code confirms the numbers:

```python
years, y, y_bgp = simulate_combined(s_old=0.10, s_new=0.40)
print(f"Growth in 2051: {100 * (y[26] / y[25] - 1):.1f}%, in 2100: {100 * (y[-1] / y[-2] - 1):.1f}%")
print(f"New BGP / old BGP: {(0.40 / 0.10) ** 0.5:.2f}   (equation 9)")
print(f"y in 2100 / new BGP: {y[-1] / y_bgp[-1]:.3f}")
```

**(b)** No. The investment rate does not appear in equation (7): long-run growth is $g_y^* = \tfrac{3}{2}\gamma\bar{n} = 3$ percent with any $\bar{s}$. A higher $\bar{s}$ raises the **level** of the path, equation (9). Growth jumps in 2051 because the capital-output ratio, $0.10/0.0809 \approx 1.24$, is far below its new BGP value from equation (8), $0.40/0.0809 \approx 4.94$. As capital builds up, the gap shrinks and growth slows down: in 2100 output per person is still 2.9 percent below the new BGP (the ratio is 0.971), so it still grows a little faster than 3 percent. South Korea followed this pattern: in our Penn World Table data, its GDP per person grew by 8.21 percent a year in 1980–1990 and by 2.26 percent a year in 2013–2023.

</details>

As in Fig. 4, the research share starts at $\bar{\ell} = 0.03$, with $\gamma = 0.6$. Adviser A proposes a new share $\bar{\ell}' = 0.15$, and adviser B proposes $\bar{\ell}' = 0.65$.

(a) With the slider, read the impact on output per person in 2050 and the long-run level effect of each plan.

(b) For each plan, find the first year in which output per person is back above the old BGP. Hover over the lines, then confirm with `simulate_romer` in the answer cell.

(c) Which plan would you recommend? Why does the bigger push not pay more in the long run?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

The title shows the impact and the level effect. In code, `simulate_romer(l_old=0.03, l_new=0.03)` gives the old BGP, and `years[(years >= 2050) & (y >= y_old)]` keeps the years from 2050 on in which the new path is at or above it. For (c), recall the hump in the Key numbers of Fig. 4.

</details>

```{python}
         l_new=FloatSlider(value=0.4, min=0.1, max=0.7, step=0.05, description="new research share ℓ̄'", style=WIDE),
```

**Source.** The model of Fig. 4 above, adapted from Fig. 6.4 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** Plan A ($\bar{\ell}' = 0.15$): output per person falls by 12.4 percent in 2050, and the new BGP is 2.30 times the old one. Plan B ($\bar{\ell}' = 0.65$): output per person falls by 63.9 percent, and the new BGP is 2.28 times the old one. The two plans have almost the same long-run payoff.

**(b)** The code finds the first year in which each path is back above the old BGP:

```python
years, y_old, y_old_bgp = simulate_romer(l_old=0.03, l_new=0.03)   # the old BGP
for l_new in [0.15, 0.65]:
    years, y, y_bgp = simulate_romer(l_old=0.03, l_new=l_new)
    back = years[(years >= 2050) & (y >= y_old)]                   # at or above the old BGP
    print(f"l' = {l_new}: impact {100 * (y[25] / y_old[25] - 1):+.1f}%, "
          f"long run x{y_bgp[-1] / y_old[-1]:.2f}, back above the old BGP in {back[0]}")
```

Plan A is back above the old path in 2052, plan B only in 2055, after a much deeper fall.

**(c)** Plan A: it delivers nearly the same long-run gain with a fifth of the fall in 2050, and it pays off sooner. The BGP level contains $(1-\bar{\ell})\,\bar{\ell}^{\gamma}$, which peaks at $\bar{\ell} = \gamma/(1+\gamma) = 0.375$. Plan B lies on the far side of the hump: there, the elasticity $\gamma - \bar{\ell}/(1-\bar{\ell}) = 0.6 - 0.65/0.35 \approx -1.26$ is negative, so the extra researchers lower the BGP, because too few people are left to make goods with the ideas. Plan A, at $0.6 - 0.15/0.85 \approx 0.42$, is still on the rising side. Moving many people out of production costs a lot of output today, and beyond the peak it buys no extra income tomorrow.

</details>

**Problem 9 (Challenge): Should China invest less?** China invested 40.5 percent of its GDP in 2024 ([World Bank, Gross capital formation (% of GDP)](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NE.GDI.TOTL.ZS?locations=CN)), and the IMF has urged it to rebalance demand toward consumption ([IMF, 2024 Article IV consultation](https://www.imf.org/en/News/Articles/2024/07/31/pr24295-china-imf-exec-board-concludes-2024-art-iv-consult)). Take a stylized version in the combined model of Fig. 8: an economy on its balanced growth path cuts its investment rate from 0.40 to a lower value in 2050. Consumption per person is what is not invested, $c_t = (1-\bar{s})\,y_t$.

(a) Set the new investment rate to 0.30. By how much is output per person lower on the new BGP, and how fast does it grow in 2051?

(b) Use equation (9) to show that on a BGP consumption per person is proportional to $(1-\bar{s})\,\bar{s}^{1/2}$. Is long-run consumption per person higher or lower after the cut to 0.30, and by how much?

(c) Find the investment rate that maximizes long-run consumption per person. Does it depend on $\gamma$, $\bar{n}$ or $\bar{d}$?

(d) What happens to consumption per person in 2050, the year of the cut, and in the years after it? Is the rebalancing a sacrifice for anyone?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

In equation (9), ask which terms change when only $\bar{s}$ changes: everything else is a constant. For (c), it is easier to maximize the log of the expression in (b). For (d), `simulate_combined` gives output per person on both paths; multiply each by its own $1-\bar{s}$.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(rise_in_s,
         s_old=fixed(0.40),
         s_new=FloatSlider(value=0.35, min=0.2, max=0.35, step=0.05, description="new investment rate s̄'", style=WIDE),
         scale=ToggleButtons(options=["ratio", "linear"], description="vertical scale"));
```

**Source.** The model of Fig. 8 above, adapted from Fig. 6.8 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The title reads "New BGP ×0.87 the old | growth 2.3% in 2051, 2.9% in 2100 (BGP: 3.0%)". On the new BGP, output per person is $(0.30/0.40)^{1/2} = 0.866$ times the old path, 13.4 percent lower, and it grows by only 2.3 percent in 2051 while the capital-output ratio falls toward its new, lower BGP value.

**(b)** In equation (9), $g_Y^* = g_y^* + \bar{n}$ depends only on $\gamma$ and $\bar{n}$ (equation 7), and $\bar{d}$, $A_t^*$ and $1-\bar{\ell}$ do not depend on $\bar{s}$ either. So $y_t^* = \text{constant}\times\bar{s}^{1/2}$, and

$$c_t^* = (1-\bar{s})\,y_t^* = \text{constant}\times(1-\bar{s})\,\bar{s}^{1/2}.$$

The cut from 0.40 to 0.30 changes long-run consumption by the factor

$$\frac{c^{*\prime}}{c^*} = \frac{0.70}{0.60}\times\left(\frac{0.30}{0.40}\right)^{1/2} = 1.1667\times0.8660 = 1.0104,$$

so consumption per person is **1.0 percent higher** in the long run, although output is 13.4 percent lower.

**(c)** Take logs: $\ln c^* = \text{constant} + \ln(1-\bar{s}) + \tfrac{1}{2}\ln\bar{s}$. Set the derivative with respect to $\bar{s}$ to zero:

$$-\frac{1}{1-\bar{s}} + \frac{1}{2\bar{s}} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2\bar{s} = 1-\bar{s} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bar{s} = \frac{1}{3}.$$

The investment rate that maximizes long-run consumption equals the exponent on capital, 1/3, whatever the values of $\gamma$, $\bar{n}$ and $\bar{d}$: they move the constant, not the shape of $(1-\bar{s})\,\bar{s}^{1/2}$. On the slider grid, 0.35 gives the highest long-run consumption (1.34 percent above the old path), just below the 1.43 percent at exactly 1/3.

**(d)** In 2050 the capital stock is given, so output does not change, and consumption jumps by $0.70/0.60 - 1 = 16.7$ percent. After that, output grows more slowly than on the old path, but consumption stays above its old path in every year: the ratio falls from 1.167 in 2050 to 1.023 in 2100 and approaches 1.010 in the long run.

```python
years, y, y_bgp = simulate_combined(s_old=0.40, s_new=0.30, last_year=2400)
years, y_old, y_old_bgp = simulate_combined(s_old=0.40, s_new=0.40, last_year=2400)
ratio = (1 - 0.30) * y / ((1 - 0.40) * y_old)          # new consumption / old consumption
print(f"Consumption ratio in 2050: {ratio[25]:.3f}, 2100: {ratio[75]:.3f}, 2400: {ratio[-1]:.3f}")
print(f"Lowest ratio from 2050 on: {ratio[25:].min():.3f}")
```

The lowest ratio from 2050 on, 1.010, comes at the very end, so consumption never falls below its old path. The rebalancing is no sacrifice for anyone in the model: with an investment rate above 1/3, the economy invests more than is worth it for consumption. The caveat is that this stylized economy starts on its balanced growth path, while China is still catching up.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

**(a)** The title reads "New BGP ×1.52 the old | growth 5.9% in 2051, 3.1% in 2100 (BGP: 3.0%)". The new BGP is $2^{0.6} \approx 1.52$ times the old one (equation 4), and output per person grows by 5.9 percent in 2051: by equation (6), ideas grow by $0.05\times2 = 10$ percent in that first year, and $1.10^{0.6} - 1 \approx 5.9$ percent.

**(b)** From equation (3), $A_t^* = \bar{z}\bar{\ell}N_t/\bar{n}$, so the yearly flow of new ideas is $\bar{z}\bar{\ell}N_t = \bar{n}A_t^*$, and $A_t^*$ grows with $N_t$: $A_{t+1}^* = (1+\bar{n})A_t^*$. Then

$$x_{t+1} = \frac{A_{t+1}}{A_{t+1}^*} = \frac{A_t + \bar{n}A_t^*}{(1+\bar{n})A_t^*} = \frac{x_t + \bar{n}}{1+\bar{n}},$$

$$1 - x_{t+1} = \frac{1 + \bar{n} - x_t - \bar{n}}{1+\bar{n}} = \frac{1 - x_t}{1+\bar{n}}.$$

The gap between the stock of ideas and its BGP value shrinks by the same factor, $1/1.05 \approx 0.952$, every year.

**(c)** After $T$ years the gap is $(1-x_{2050})/(1+\bar{n})^T$. Half of it is closed when $(1+\bar{n})^T = 2$, that is after

$$T = \frac{\ln 2}{\ln(1+\bar{n})} = \frac{0.693}{0.0488} \approx 14.2 \text{ years},$$

so by 2065. Neither $\bar{z}'$ nor $\gamma$ appears: the speed at which the gap in ideas closes depends only on $\bar{n}$, the growth of the research workforce.

**(d)** Output per person is within 10 percent of its new BGP when $x_t^{0.6} \geq 0.9$, that is $x_t \geq 0.9^{1/0.6} = 0.839$, or a gap $1 - x_t \leq 0.161$. With $\bar{z}' = 2$, $x_{2050} = 1/2$ and the gap starts at 0.5, so we need $1.05^T \geq 0.5/0.161$, $T \geq 23.2$: the year **2074**. With $\bar{z}' = 8$, the gap starts at $1 - 1/8 = 0.875$, so $T \geq 34.7$: the year **2085**.

```python
for z_new in [2.0, 8.0]:
    years, y, y_bgp = simulate_romer(z_new=z_new)
    close = years[(years >= 2050) & (y >= 0.9 * y_bgp)]      # within 10% of the new BGP
    print(f"z' = {z_new}: within 10% of the new BGP from {close[0]}")
print(f"Half-life of the gap in ideas: {np.log(2) / np.log(1.05):.1f} years")
```

**(e)** No. With $\bar{z}' = 2$, after ten years the gap in ideas is still $0.5/1.05^{10} = 0.307$, so output per person is $0.693^{0.6} \approx 0.80$ times its new BGP: about 42 percent of the long-run gain has arrived (output is 1.22 times the old path, out of an eventual 1.52). Because the gap closes by only $1 - 1/1.05$, less than 5 percent, each year whatever the size of the boost, the full gains of a better research technology take decades, not years.
